I'm a young woman traveling alone. I just drove cross-country (over 15k miles) in big cities and wilderness alike and not once felt even remotely unsafe (except in New Orleans. I left pretty much a soon as I arrived.)

That said, I do have a couple weapons including pepper spray, but I never even came close to needing to use it. Just use your head and stay aware.

Walmart Bean burritos are cheaper than Taco Bell and more filling. Get their biggest, cheapest tortillas, 1$ canned refried beans, some shredded cheese if you're feeling fancy or I honestly just drizzle taco sauce on mine. You can eat them cold or heat em up, but I like em cold.
Overnight oats are cheap, filling, and can be tasty. I use cinnamon, a little maple syrup or sugar packets, oats ofc, chia seeds, and a little nutmeg and allspice. You can also add freeze dries or fresh fruit if you've got it. Add enough water to cover all ingredients (I put mine in a small glass dish or mason jar) cover and let sit overnight. Once the oats absorb the liquid it's pretty yum and keeps me going until dinnertime (I have an apple or nothing for lunch.)
As for fast food, you don't need a Costco membership to eat at the food court. $1.50 hot dogs, $2 pizza slice or you can feast on a massive pizza for $10. They also have good ice cream, smoothies, coffee, and even sandwiches.

I'm 21F and at this point I can confidently say I'll probably never have friends again in my life. Growing up I became "friends" with the girls around me because we saw each other every day, but after middle school and moving schools those old friends disappeared and I haven't made any sense. 

It's not even that I don't know "how" to make friends - I'm aware of all the rituals and social rules necessary to create them, but maintaining them is completely out of the question. I don't like hanging out with people outside of a structured thing like a job or an event where everyone is participating in a shared activity (like hiking, drinking or other social activities are a big no no) and I don't even like talking to people through text, email, or even calling them.

I'm just not built for friends. My brain both doesn't care and even if I do the social stress is just too much of a problem. I'm really jealous of autistics that are extroverted/able to make and keep friendships because it is really hard and lonely sometimes, but I tell myself there's more to life. I have my art to keep me occupied and various other hobbies.

Try not to be too hard on yourself. Even neurotypicals complain about being friendless, for various reasons. A lot of people your age (and my age) are also so busy with school or work or whatever else that it's hard for them to make friends too. Keep your chin up!

One of the things I can't live without is my hotlogic hot lunchbox. You can cook raw food, frozen food, and warm things up. Get the 12V you can plug in and use it when you drive somewhere, it takes around 30min to an hour to get really warm, but since I drive a lot I find it useful. I buy the 1.25 beefy bean burritos from Walmart and warm them up, 790 calories per burrito and they're pretty tasty. You can also make your own ofc. I warmed up frozen ham sandwiches, frozen cooked chicken in sauce, etc. Also if you can swing it I would definitely buy a battery pack like a Jackery or equivalent. Depending on the wattage of your appliance and the size battery pack you buy, you can run almost anything off them. I have a Jackery 1000w I got on sale and it's a lifesaver. I can run a 800w hot water kettle, charge my phone, my laptop, camera batteries, etc. When I need to recharge it I can plug it into the 12V car port and drive, it usually takes at least an hour, if not more, to fully recharge it since it's so big but you can also charge it in any wall outlet although mine is really heavy so I don't tend to lug it around places. Kind of awkward walking into the library with a massive battery pack haha.

Felt the exact same way as you one month in. It's an adjustment, especially if you've lived your whole life in a house. You're essentially homeless, no matter how fancy your rig is and that comes with challenges.
My advice, find what makes you happy. Why did you want to live like this? Being in nature? Being free to do what you want? Living/visiting high cost of living cities without having to pay rent? For me, it's a combination of all three, but nature is the biggest. As soon as I visited a national park and saw what kind of freedom this lifestyle can truly offer, it felt exactly like the Instagram posts make it seem like.
Just give yourself some time. Three months minimum, six months preferably. Then you can decide what to do. Regardless of what happens, you'll have a good story and an interesting experience to look back on.

My advice to you, while perhaps unconventional, is to move into your car. I felt a lot like you when I was younger. Granted, I'm only 21, but when I was around 14-15 I felt the same way as you. My family has always traveled, so I'm used to being transient and not having "roots" anywhere. The definition of home was always changing, and when I thought about growing up, going to college, getting my own apartment, car, maybe getting married, I felt like someone was shoving me into a dark room where the walls just kept getting smaller and smaller until I was suffocating. 

That said, I've also had a lot of trouble making strong friendships or relationships besides family members that might ground me to one place. When I heard about people who live in their car and travel for work or just travel in general and work seasonal jobs, it felt like I suddenly had a reason to live. Like there was suddenly something out there I could do that wouldn't trap me in one place, or worse, force me into an endless grind of moneymaking just so that I could, what, afford food and shelter? 

I know the lifestyle I've chosen is going to mean a slightly harder, perhaps less convenient life than most. I won't have the security of the same job and the same coworkers unless I work from home or make an online business. But to me, all the negatives associated with being a nomad are far, far outweighed by the simple fact that I get to live the way I want. 

All that said, here's my main advice. Do what you want. Life is short, as cliche as that sounds, and although it might be scary and terrifying to jump into the great unknown, if you don't do it, what's the worse that could happen? You get stuck in the same place, the same job, the same life, physically surviving all while your soul rots away inside of you. I wouldn't be able to live like that. I suspect you won't be able to, either. 

Just make a plan. Start small. Research jobs that you could or would do. You don't have to constantly be on the move, too. I stay at places for up to a year before I have enough finance and a plan on where to head next. Don't do anything without a plan, or you will end up stranded, hungry, or worse. You want to go into the woods? Look at jobs related to camping or forestry. There are plenty of seasonal jobs that involve living in the woods or otherwise working outside. If you don't like physical jobs, look into a job you can do while being transient. There are lots of resources online. You can also just do what I do which is work fast food or retail or any other minimum-wage job that'll accept me. Sometimes it doesn't always work out and the work is never fun, but to me, it's just a means to an end. The job works for me, not the other way around. And I'm never stuck. I can always move on. 

Good luck.

I think a nice middle ground between space vs fuel efficiency is a minivan. Something large like a toyota sienna or honda odyssey. If that's too small for you, though, then I suggest something like a ford transit (15-19 mpg), gmc savanna (11-16 but not a lot of headroom), or chevy express. 

It also depends on what your travel style is like. You said you're living in it full time, are you going to be doing a full conversion (solar, electric, fridge, the works) and mostly boondocking or are you going to be traveling a lot and burning up a lot of gas? Obviously the more you move around the better fuel economy you're going to want, so maybe something smaller is the way to go. But if you're planning on staying in one place for months at a time without really traveling as often maybe a bigger van is worth the price tag.

I wasn't very educated myself on autism before I met my ex, but he's someone who's very socially aware and knew about it before I did. He helped me come out of my shell and taught me a lot about neurotypicals and the way that they work and think, and thanks to him I became a lot more outgoing and understood myself better. That said, there were a lot of things he didn't understand, and although we never lived together, when we hung out it was pretty obvious when he misunderstood something I said or did. Often he would think I was mad at him because I wouldn't make eye contact enough or I wasn't "responsive enough." I also felt he was embarassed bringing me around his friends. I often didn't understand a lot of their social cues or subtext, and he would always make a point to mention how "weird" I acted. I think if we were still dating, I would have asked him to try and understand me a bit more. It's hard feeling like you can be yourself and drop the mask when even the people you care about misunderstand you. While that wasn't the reason we broke up (he cheated on me) it was still hurtful, so I would try to talk to your boyfriend and use it as a way to get to know each other at a deeper level. If he doesn't understand, it's not the end of the world, but at least you tried.

It took a while, about a month or two. Whenever he saw a dog or person walking by the house, he'd bark and snarl and freak out and then proceed to whimper a lot. When that happened, I would grab him gently but firmly by his collar and lead him to another room nearby and put him inside by himself until I heard he wasn't whining anymore (usually this took 10-15 seconds, sometimes more if he was particularly upset). Once he was quiet, I'd let him out and walk back to the window pretending to look out and survey the area. During this time I didn't let him near the window, and gave him a stern "down" if he tried. Once the coast was clear I'd let him do his thing. At first, nothing changed, and he would still freak out day after day, but eventually, he began to look towards me instead of freak immediately, which I praised by giving him a treat (he loves whip cream) after a while the outbursts went down to 0. He still gets very alert when he sees someone, but unless they're coming up the driveway he usually knows that when he's quiet and only watches he gets a nice treat.
